description_block:
The present vase is a fine example of the distinctive marbled wares produced during the Tang dynasty. Known in Chinese as jiao tai, the technique involved twisting and kneading together differently coloured clays to create irregular swirling patterns, the effect here enhanced by a transparent glaze. Fragments of such wares have been excavated at the Gongxian kilns at Huangye, Henan province, illustrated in Three-Colour Glazed Pottery Kilns of the Tang Dynasty at Huangye, Beijing, 2000, pl. 71, no. 9, as well as at the Liquanfang kilns in Xi'an, Shaanxi province, published in The Kiln Site of Tricolor-Glazed Pottery at Liquanfang in Chang'an Capital City of Tang Dynasty, Beijing, 2008, pl. 39, attesting to the production of marbled wares during the period.
Marbled wares were produced in a variety of forms, including bowls, jars and pillows, but vases appear to be particularly rare. For a Tang vessel of closely related form, compare a straw-glazed stoneware bottle vase, similarly modelled with a bulbous body rising to a tall, slender neck with a flared mouth, formerly in the Florence and Herbert Irving Collection, sold at Christieâs New York, 21st March 2019, lot 1229.

description_block:
This rare cup, with its subtle guan glaze so admired during the Southern Song dynasty, exemplifies the understated aesthetic favoured by the cultured scholar-officials of the period. The present vessel can be attributed to one of the guan ('official') kilns established at Hangzhou, the Southern Song capital, to supply ceramics for the court following the relocation of the imperial house to the South in 1127, when access to the celebrated northern manufactories, including the Ru kilns at Baofeng in Henan, was lost. The Jiaotanxia ('Below the Suburban Altar') kilns, believed to have produced wares such as this cup for the court, have tentatively been identified with kiln sites discovered at Wuguishan, south of Hangzhou.
Compare a similar guan celadon-glazed cup of the same size, described as a brushwasher, exhibited in The Arts of the Sung Dynasty, vol. 32, Oriental Ceramic Society, London, 1959, cat. no. 164; and another related example in the National Museum of Asian Art, Washington, D.C., illustrated in Oriental Ceramics: The World's Great Collections, vol. 9, Tokyo, 1981, pl. 45. See also a similar 'Jiaotanxia' guan bowl offered in these rooms, 9th November 2005, lot 270; and a Longquan celadon cup imitating 'Jiaotanxia' guan ware, of closely related form and size, in the Huzhou City Museum, illustrated in Zhongguo taoci quanji, vol. 8, Shanghai, 1999, pl. 65.

description_block:
Bursting with vitality, deftly carved by a practiced hand, the present meiping represents one of the finest displays of Cizhou sgraffiato still preserved in private hands.
Beyond the subtle elegance of its bulbous meiping (prunus vase) form, the present vase is most notable for the quality of its dramatic bichromatic design. In vogue from the late eleventh century through to the twelfth century, the technique responsible for this vibrant design is one of the most intricate ever devised among early ceramicists. Coating the form in successive layers of white and black slip (a thin liquified clay), the craftsmen would then carefully incise their vibrant floral designs, scraping back the black slip to reveal the pristine white below and rendering a bold contrast; more akin to an ink painting than a vase surface. While several kiln centres around Cizhou are known to have been in production during the period, examples of this exquisite quality and complex technique appear to mostly have been produced at the centre of the region around Guantai; compare a sherd uncovered from a Guantai site of closely related sgraffiato peony design in Yutaka Mino, The Cizhou Kiln at Guantai, Beijing, 1997, col. pl. 21, fig. 96.
Meiping of comparable size, elegant proportions and magnificent carving are exceedingly rare and almost all preserved in public institutions. The most closely related known example in private hands remains the meiping from the collection of Dikran Khan KÃ©lÃ©kian (1868-1951), most recently sold as part of the Ise Collection in our Hong Kong rooms, 9th September 2025, lot 5008, of more slender proportions but closely comparable in size and design of scrolling peonies and lappet borders (Fig. 1). Two further meiping in the Yamato Bukakan, Nara and Tokyo National Museum, Tokyo, both more slender than the present example, similarly share the present peony design and are illustrated in Toji taikei, vol. 39: Jishuyo [Cizhou ware], Tokyo, 1974, pls 42 and 43; and again in Freedom of Clay and Brush through Seven Centuries in Northern China: Tz'u-chou Type Wares, 960-1600 A.D., Indianapolis Museum of Art, 1981, figs 98 and 97, alongside three other semi-slender examples from the Worcester Art Museum, pl. 39; the former royal House of Yi, Seoul, fig. 99; and the British Museum, London (fig. 100, accession no. 1968,0422.25), the latter more similar in proportions to the present.
Also compare an example in the Kyoto National Museum, illustrated alongside the KÃ©lÃ©kian meiping in Charm of Black & White Ware: Transition of Cizhou Type Wares, Osaka Municipal Museum of Art, 2002, cat. nos 51 and 52; a more freely incised meiping with different borders in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, illustrated in Wu Tung, Earth Transformed Chinese Ceramics in the Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 2001, p. 63; and another in the Asia Society, New York, in Treasures of Asian Art: The Asia Society's Mr. and Mrs. John D. The present dish, featuring a layer of vibrant green glaze over a freely carved black slip design represents the apogee of production at the Cizhou kilns of northern China. Centred around kiln sites in Guantai, the Cizhou potters of the 12th century produced a wide range of remarkable and innovative designs, of which green glazed pieces are among the rarest and most desirable.

description_block:
This remarkable jar possesses all of the hallmarks of imperial Longquan. Of rich green tone, suffused by crackles after generations of treasured ownership, the jar stands as tribute to the exacting standards of the early Ming court and the enduring beauty of celadon.
Known as 'pomegranate jars' (shiliuzun), the present form carries features of Tibetan Buddhist metal bum-pa vessels, with its folded rim, slightly drooping edge, and raised boss decoration. In the early Ming, the court adopted a conciliatory policy toward Tibetan Buddhism, with the Yongle Emperor in particular repeatedly dispatching envoys to Lhasa with lavish gifts. Ceramics, as a precious present, was an important part of these tribute lists. The serene glaze colour and sturdy body of Longquan celadon met both the aesthetic preferences and practical needs of the Tibetan region.
Comparable examples of this form are extremely rare, with fewer than ten comparable examples apparently extant, and most with heavily moulded floral designs. A similarly plain and refined example of smaller size from the Qing Court Collection, now preserved in the Palace Museum, Beijing (accession no. æ145048) is illustrated in Longquan of the World: Longquan Celadon and Globalization, vol. II: State Vessels, Beijing, 2019, cat. no. 108 (alongside a moulded example, cat. no. 109). description_block:
Exceptional for its monumental scale, powerful modelling and rare dark-brown glaze, the present horse is a particularly striking example of Tang dynasty ceramic sculpture. Standing 79 cm high, the figure is masterfully modelled with a muscular body supported on long, powerful legs, its robust proportions conveying both strength and vitality. Its commanding presence is further enhanced by the rich dark-brown glaze, while the contrasting amber-glazed saddle and trappings provide a vivid counterpoint to the horse's dark coat. 
Horses occupied a privileged position in Tang society, where they were potent symbols of wealth, rank and power, their representation in elite tombs reflecting the status and importance of the deceased. Ownership of horses was itself a mark of social distinction: as early as 667, a sumptuary law restricted the right to own horses, excluding artisans and tradesmen from this privilege. While Tang horses are more commonly encountered in the characteristic amber, cream and green tones of the sancai palette, dark brown or black-glazed examples are considerably rarer. Notably, several surviving examples of this rare type are, like the present horse, distinguished by their unusually large size. 
Compare two horses excavated in 1995 from the Tang tomb of Prince Jiemin-Li Chongjun in Fuping county, one covered in a matte-brown glaze with a sancai-glazed saddle and the other in a brown glaze with an ochre-coloured saddle, illustrated in National Treasure â Collection of Rare Cultural Relics of Shaanxi Province, Xi'an, 1998, pp. 183-84; and a black-glazed horse in the Luoyang Museum, illustrated in Da Sancai, Sancai from Luoyang Museum and the Liaoning Provincial Museum, 1989, no. 11. Among the most celebrated examples is the monumental black-glazed horse formerly in the British Rail Pension Fund Collection, sold in these rooms, 12th December 1989, lot 56. Compare also the magnificent and extremely rare bowing horse from the Cindy and Jay Pritzker Collection, sold in our New York rooms, 25th March 2026, lot 161, which, while differing in its dynamic pose and elaborate trappings, is similarly distinguished by its rare dark glaze and imposing scale. See also another black-glazed horse with a cream-coloured mane and elaborate breast straps, sold together with a chestnut-glazed horse in our New York rooms, 27th March 2003, lot 36, and again 17th September 2013, lot 45.
The dating of this lot is consistent with the results of thermoluminescence test, Oxford Authentication Ltd., no. C125g53.

This bowl is a very rare and unusual example of a well-known group of imperial wares. Bowls with this type of lush flower decoration on a coral-red ground, which were made around the late Kangxi and early Yongzheng period and revived in the Qianlong reign, are known with Kangxi and Yongzheng yu zhi, Yongzheng nian zhi, six-character Yongzheng marks; and Qianlong seal marks. Examples of these various types, all smaller in size, taller in proportion and flared, are illustrated in The Tsui Museum of Art. A similar large bowl from the British Rail Pension Fund, sold in our Hong Kong rooms, 16th May 1989, lot 73, is illustrated in Sotheby's. Thirty Years in Hong Kong, Hong Kong, 2003, pl. 318.  
The use of the phrase yu zhi [made to imperial order] suggests a closer relationship to the imperial court than the regular wording nian zhi [made in the period of...] and follows the style of marking used at the imperial enamelling workshops in Beijing, which applied yu zhi marks in enamel colours.

description_block:
Imperial porcelain dishes decorated with green-enamelled dragons first appeared during the Chenghua period, and continued to be produced throughout the later Ming dynasty, particularly during the Hongzhi and Zhengde reigns. The enduring popularity of the design established the 'green dragon' dish as one of the classic types of porcelain produced for the imperial court. While on most Qing dynasty examples the dragons were simply painted in green enamel over the glaze, on Ming dishes such as the present piece the design was first incised and reserved in the biscuit during the initial firing, before the dragon silhouettes were filled with green enamel and fired a second time. This additional process lends the decoration a subtle three-dimensional quality.
Closely related Zhengde dishes are preserved in important museum and private collections. Compare similar examples preserved in the British Museum, London, illustrated in Jessica Harrison-Hall, Ming Ceramics in the British Museum, London, 2001, pls 8:33-35; and another in the Shanghai Museum, Shanghai, illustrated in Lu Minghua, Shanghai Bowuguan zangpin yanjiu daxi / Studies of the Shanghai Museum Collections: A Series of Monographs. Mingdai guanyao ciqi [Ming Imperial Porcelain], Shanghai, 2007, pl. 1-44. See also a dish of the same size and design from the Leshantang Collection, illustrated in The Leshantang Collection of Chinese Porcelain, Taipei, 2005, pl. 18, and sold in our Hong Kong rooms, 9th April 2024, lot 112; and another from the British Rail Pension Fund, sold three times in these rooms, 13th December 1966, lot 73; 1st July 1969, lot 149; and 17th November 1970, lot 76; and subsequently in our Hong Kong rooms, 16th May 1989, lot 27. This fine and rare stem bowl is pristine in colour, elegant in shape, and adorned with exacting incised decoration. Akin to the anhua ('hidden decoration') technique first employed in the early Ming dynasty, the present bowl represents the reinterpretation of classic designs through the eyes of the Yongzheng Emperor (r. 1723-1735). The Three Emperors. 1662-1795, Royal Academy of Arts, London, 2005, cat. no. 169, p. 255 bottom right.

description_block:
Jars of this form, delicately painted in the doucai palette with chrysanthemum and lotus motifs, were inspired by porcelain produced during the Chenghua period, whose celebrated wares were particularly prized at the Qianlong court. While no Chenghua prototype of precisely this design appears to be recorded, jars employing a similar decorative vocabulary are known, including an example from the Qing Court Collection, painted with chrysanthemum medallions and butterflies, illustrated in The Complete Collection of Treasures of the Palace Museum. Porcelains in Polychrome and Contrasting Colours, Hong Kong, 1999, pl. 166. The particular esteem in which Chenghua wares were held at the Qianlong court is further documented in the imperial workshop archives, Qinggong neiwufu zaobanchu dang'an zonghui [General Collection of Archival Records from the Qing Imperial Household Department Workshop]. In 1748, the Qianlong Emperor ordered Tang Ying (1682-1756), superintendent of the imperial kilns at Jingdezhen, to produce replacement covers for a group of treasured Ming porcelains, including a Chenghua wucai jar decorated with chrysanthemums. Significantly, only copies of these prized vessels were permitted to be sent to Jiangxi, while the originals remained in the imperial collection.  
Similar Qianlong jars and covers are preserved in important museum collections. Compare a pair in the Tianjin Museum, Tianjin, illustrated in Tianjin shi yishu bowuguan cang ci [Porcelains from the Tianjin Municipal Museum], Hong Kong, 1993, pl. 177; another pair included in the exhibition Min Shin no Bijutsu [Ming and Qing Art], Osaka City Museum of Fine Arts, Osaka, 1980, cat. no. 1-192; and a single jar and cover preserved in the National Palace Museum, Taipei, published in Catalogue of Châing Dynasty Porcelain, vol. 2, Tokyo, 1981, pl. 24. description_block:
Of slender form; crisply cast with a swirling profusion of zoomorphic designs in mixed-relief, the present vessel is a classical example of the austere magnificence of Late Shang casting. Inscribed with a rare and important clan sign and preserved for at least a century in private collections, the vessel possesses all the hallmarks of an exemplary bronze, from its fine casting quality to its smooth even and dark time-worn patina.
Beaker vessels, known to connoisseurs as gu, represent one of the important and prolific bronze wares produced in the Shang dynasty. Commonly used by elite families and ritual practitioners as vessels for storing wine for ecstatic rituals, gu of this form are among the most frequently attested wares in royal burial contexts. The present gu is particularly fine in the quality of its material and casting, with its complex design of taotie masks, kui dragons and cicada blades rendered against a ground of tight leiwen keyfrets. A bronze gu with very similar decoration and design, excavated from a Shang dynasty tomb in Mangzhang, Luoshan, Xinyang, Henan in 1980, is illustrated in Zhongguo qingtong qi quanji [Complete collection of bronze wares in China], vol. 4, Beijing, 1998, pl. 68; another was found in the excavation of Tomb M2046 in Xibeigang, Anyang, Henan during the Republican period, and illustrated in Li Chi et al., eds, Yinxu chutu qingtong gu xing qi zhi yanjiu / Studies of the Bronze Ku-Beaker Excavated from Hsiao TÃºn & Hou Chia Chuang, Taipei, 1964, pl. 32; and a third example of Shi å²clan mark from the WessÃ©n Collection, closely related but for snakes in the the upper register in place of the present dragons, was included in Ancient Chinese Bronzes from the Stoclet and WessÃ©n Collections, Eskenazi, London, 1975, cat. no. 1.
The present gu is particularly noteworthy in its rare pictogram cast on the wall of the interior. Depicting a ge dagger-axe cutting off an ear, the insignia â generally glossed as Guo èâ is recorded in the famous second century dictionary the Shuowen Jiezi [Explaining and analysing characters], where scholar Xu Shen explains that ears were cut off from bodies of enemies in ancient times as a way to claim merit. Surviving examples of bronze vessels from the Guo clan rarely survive outside of archaeological contexts or public insitutions. Compare a bronze jue (M21:3) bearing the same clan insignia from Phase III of Anyang period, uncovered in 1991 from the excavation of Tomb M21 in Hougang, Anyang, Henan, illustrated in â1991 nian Anyang Hougang Yin mu de fajueâ Kaogu, 1993:10, pl. 26:4 & 29:5; and a jue of the same clan mark and very closely related mixed-relief casting style, possible produced as part of the same commission as the present gu, preserved in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (accession no. 49.135.15) and illustrated on the Museum's website; and a gu, very closely related to the present vessel in clan mark and design but with the addition of flanges to the neck, now preserved in the Indianapolis Museum of Art, Indianapolis (accession no. 48.115), included in Beauty and Tranquility: The Eli Lily Collection of Chinese Art, Indianapolis Museum of Art, Indianapolis, 1983, cat. no. 23.

Of deep heavily adorned sides and a tall tapered taotie foot, the present vessel is a fine example of the rare yu vessel form and a classical example of late Shang decoration in its austerity and grandeur. From the whorls and taotie masks complementing the flared rim to the bold series of mammiform bosses around the body, the present yu is a triumph of bronze-age workmanship.
Rarely attested in the archaeological record, the yu form appears to have emerged in modern-day Shaanxi province with the present âdiamond-and-bossâ design variation likely an innovation by the foundries of the royal Shang capital of Anyang. While contemporaneous sources on the yu are rare, their function likely corresponded to the more commonplace gui vessels of the Western Zhou dynasty, which essentially follow yu in proportions and surface decorations but with the addition of two or more handles.
Compare a series of related yu including those preserved in the National Museum of Asian Art, Washington, in Robert Bagley, Shang Ritual Bronzes in the Arthur M. Sackler Collections, Washington, 1987, pl. 98; figs 98.3-5; pls 100 and 101; figs 100.1-3; and figs 101.1-2. Another related yu but with stylised kui dragons in the upper register in place of the present whorls from the Mount Trust Collection, illustrated in The Mount Trust Collection of Chinese Art, Victoria and Albert Museum, London, 1970, cat. no. 2 and sold from the Sze Yuan Tang collection of Anthony Hardy at Christieâs New York, 16th September 2010, lot 826; and another from the Morse Collection with a more dense band of whorls, included in Spirit and Ritual; The Morse Collection of Ancient Chinese Art, Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, 1982, cat. no. 5, and sold at Christieâs New York, 19th March 2008, lot 493.

Poised on three sturdy zoomorphic legs, its flattened belly finely cast with swirling designs, surmounted with crisp openwork ridges and a fearsome dragon spout, the present ewer is typical of the inventive designs which emerged during the height of the Eastern Zhou dynasty with the advent of loss-wax casting.
Rippling with life and ancient power, the present ewer, termed he by connoisseurs, was produced for an elite context where it was used to serve wine, likely in ritual contexts.
Comparable examples of this casting quality and design are rare. Compare an almost identical ewer of the same design and inscription - possibly the pair to the present, preserved in the Poly Art Museum, Beijing, illustrated in Selected Bronzes in the Collection of the Poly Art Museum, Beijing, 1999, p. 226, where Wang Shiming identifies the first character as a clan name and associates the design with elite families from the ancient State of Chu. Also compare a pair of closely related he of slightly more complex handle and flange design uncovered in 1978 from two late Spring and Autumn period tombs in Xiasi temple, Xichuan, Henan, illustrated in Zhongguo qingtong qi quanji, vol. 4, Beijing, 1998, pls 62 and 63; and a third he, more florid still, uncovered in 1977 from a Warring States context at Nanmendong, Luoding, Guangdong, illustrated ibid., vol. 5, pl. 131.

description_block:
This pair of superbly cast and detailed fittings would once have been fitted to a crossbow or acted or supported a crossbow on a chariot for a high-ranking charioteer. Fittings of this type have been excavated in pairs in association with chariots, but the actual function and placement has been debated amongst scholars with one theory proposing that they were fitted to the front of a crossbow shaft to support a bow with the upcurved terminals acting as the aiming mechanism (Luoyang Museum, 'Luoyang Zhongzhoulu Zhanguo chemakeng [The Chariot Pit Found at Zhongzhou Road, Luoyang]', Kaogu, vol. 3, 1974, p. 177, fig. 7). Another â perhaps more commonly accepted â theory is that the fittings functioned as crossbow supports on a chariot. They were attached horizontally to the front panel of a chariot, adjacent to the occupants. The crossbow would have been placed facing down, with its bow resting on the curved shafts and its handle positioned obliquely upward, ready at hand for a quick draw.
Compare a related fitting with the terminal of the curved shaft similarly rendered in the form of a snake's head, but decorated with silver inlay only, excavated in Luoyang in 1973 and now preserved in the Luoyang Museum, illustrated in Li Xueqin, ed., Zhongguo meishu quanji: Gongyi meishu bian [Complete series on Chinese art: Arts and crafts section], 5: Qingtong qi [Bronzes], vol. 2, Beijing, 1986, pl. 117. Compare also another pair of gold and silver-inlaid bronze fittings sold in our Hong Kong rooms, 25th November 2022, lot 875.

description_block:
As ritual power shifted from the hands of kings and shamans to those of local elites, the Han dynasty (202 BCE - 220 CE) witnessed a radical shift in the production of ritual vessels. Moving beyond the austere and imposing designs of the Shang and Western Zhou and the more florid geometric developments of the Eastern Zhou, Han bronzes possess an almost secular elegance in their proportions, slender designs and surface decoration. Here exemplified by three vessels, unadorned but for subtly cast details, bow-string bands and taotie handles, this remarkable assemblage shines with ancient splendour, coated in a thick layer of gilding still brilliant after two millennia. 
Individual examples of this superb gilt surface were apparently limited only to the most elite funerary contexts and very rarely survive, let alone preserved in a group of three. Compare a related gilt hu vase â also known as a zhong wine jar â unearthed from the tomb of the King of Nanyue in Guangzhou, Western Han dynasty, illustrated in Zhongguo qingtongqi quanji [Complete collection of Chinese bronze vessels], vol. 19, Beijing, 2019, pl. 239; another in the Palace Museum, Beijing, in Gugong qingtong tudian / Illustrated Catalogue of Bronzes in the Palace Museum, Beijing, 2010, pl. 207; and another sold from the collection of the Okada Museum of Art in our Hong Kong rooms, 22nd November 2025, lot 1088. A closely related flattened bianhu flask from the Maclean Collection was sold in our New York rooms, 23rd March 2022, lot 249; and a ding tripod of more fragmentary gilt and silvered surface sold in our Hong Kong rooms, 18th October 2023, lot 531.

description_block:
Tang dynasty spherical censers, known as xiangnang, were sophisticated incense burners designed as openwork metal spheres with an internal gimbal-like suspension system that kept the burning incense upright regardless of how the outer shell moved. See the article written by Bing Huang, âThe Religious and Technological History of the Tang Dynasty Spherical Incense Burnerâ, Religions, 2022, 13, no. 482, where the author discusses its development and illustrates the famous gilt-silver examples excavated at Famen Temple, fig. 1, and preserved in the Shosoin, Todai-ji Temple, Nara, fig. 2.
Beyond their practical use, spherical incensers had important religious and cultural significance. Incense burning in Tang Buddhism and elite society was associated with ritual practice, refinement, and communication with the spiritual realm. The article argues that the technology embodied in these censers spread westward through intercultural exchanges along trade networks, influencing related devices in the Islamic world and later Venice, making the Tang spherical censer notable not only as a religious artifact but also as an important example of early technological innovation.

description_block:
Rippling with life, draped in soft fabrics that gather at a knot across the chest and fold gently along the legs, the present fragment represents a serene yet striking example of the figural arts produced during the first half of sixth century.
While the identity of the present figure might be thought obscured by its fragmentary nature, the soft folds of its robes, its grand posture and the myriad Budhhas to its reverse confirm the figure's identity as the Buddha himself. Two dated steles similarly representing the historical Buddha help to confirm the present attribution, exhibiting the softer more curved treatment of the robes distinctive of Eastern Wei in contrast to the sharper, rigid style of Northern Wei: one in the Museum Reitberg, Zurich, illustrated in Osvald SirÃ©n, Chinese Sculptures in the von der Heydt Collection, Zurich, 1959, cat. no. 22, dated in accordance with 536; and the other in the Cleveland Museum of Art, illustrated in Hai-Wai Yi-Chen. Chinese Art in Overseas Collections, Buddhist Sculpture II, Taipei, 1990, pl. 34, dated in accordance with 537. These figures, sharing the same characteristic dark limestone typical of Eastern Wei centres in Henan, also show the distinct knotting of the garment across the chest falling to the waist. Another fragment of closely related stone, sculptural quality and Myriad Buddha reverse is attested and likely derived from the same stele as the present, exhibited from the Ching-ya Tâang Collection in The Art of Contemplation - Religious Sculpture from Private Collections, National Palace Museum, Taipei, 1997, p. 80, cat. no. 13.

description_block:
Gazing down in calm benevolence, adorned with an elaborate princely headdress, the present head is a magnificent example of the great transition of Chinese figural arts around the turn of the seventh century. The face plumply rendered and pooling slightly below the chin, the slanting eyes widely set and crisply hewn in quiet contemplation, the lips and nose sweetly poised; this head is typical of the Sui dynasty (581-618) â a period of dramatic reform from the austerity of earlier sculpting styles to the more exaggerated naturalism of the ensuing Tang (618-907).
Related heads of this period with similarly rounded and substantial features from the Northern Qi and Sui dynasties have been uncovered from sites in Qingzhou, Shandong, and are sometimes likened to those of the Indian Gupta period, the raw features and sturdy carving of which are evident in the present head, yet to be fully assimilated into the smooth naturalism of the Tang. Compare several such figures, sharing the elaborate tasseled headdresses and heavy features of the present, included in Return of the Buddha. The Qingzhou Discoveries, Royal Academy of Arts, London, 2002, particularly cat. nos 29 and 31; and others preserved in Sui dynasty contexts in Shanxi province in Osvad SirÃ©n, Chinese Sculpture from the Fifth to the Fourteenth Century, vol. II, London, 1925, pls 303A and B, 316 and 329. 
For further examples of this quintessential Sui style in important public institutions compare three related figures included in SaburÅ Matsubara, ChÅ«goku BukkyÅ chÅkoku shiron [History of Chinese Buddhist sculpture], vol. description_block: This elegant bronze sculpture of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, depicted standing in tribhanga on a waisted lotus pedestal and stepped hexagonal base, is adorned in a long dhoti and fluttering scarves. The contours of the slender body are well defined in the contrapposto silhouette and the wet-drapery effect of the clothing, all of which are characteristic of Buddhist sculpture in the high Tang dynasty. The curving form of the deityâs torso achieves an almost dance-like movement. This highly recognisable stylistic element of the swayed-hip posture became especially popular during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong (712-756), when sculptures in general became more dynamic in their design.

description_block:
Buddhism had already established itself as the de facto religion of Yunnan by the late 9th century with the arrival of Azhali Buddhism from India. This esoteric sect, in which scholarly acharyas would lead the community and perform spells and mantras for the nationâs protection, was adopted as the state religion of the southwestern Kingdom of Nanzhao by its final Emperor Shunhuazhen (r. 897â902) at the very end of the ninth century. Nanzhao, which had flourished in southwestern China and northern Southeast Asia in the eighth and ninth centuries, was overthrown in 902 CE and, following decades of uncertainty, the Duan family, under Duan Siping, took up the mantle of Azhali. Uniting Nanzhao sympathizers to overthrow a series of usurping kings in 937, Duan Siping declared himself Emperor Taizu and gave his empire the Buddhist name Dali â âGreat Ruling Principle.â The Emperors of Dali embraced the Buddhism of their predecessors with open arms and relied on its principles and rituals to legitimize their reign. Indeed, following their reigns, ten of Daliâs twenty-two emperors are said to have retired as monks out of genuine religious reverence.
This superb bell, cast on each side at the handle with an intricate depiction of Prajnaparamita, is much rarer than the more commonly found bronze figures created in the Dali Kingdom, especially those depicting Acouye Guanyin. The heads of Prajnaparamita share the same slender but serene features found on the faces of the complete figures. For other ritual objects emanating from the Dali Kingdom, see a gilt-bronze kila depicting a single-faced bodhisattva, excavated from the pagoda of Chongsheng Temple in Yunnan, currently in the Yunnan Provincial Museum Collection, illustrated in Li Kunsheng, The Complete Works of Yunnan National Fine Arts: The Sculpture and Painting Arts of Nanzhao and Dali Kingdoms, Kunming, 1999, pl. 298, and another kila cast with three-headed Vidyaraja, sold at Christieâs Hong Kong, 29th May 2019, lot 2711.

description_block:
Buddha Shakyamuni is seated in vajraparyankasana on a double lotus throne fitted with a reticulated wood stand carved with stylised dragons and flaming pearl. The Buddha extends his right hand in bhumisparsha mudra, with the left remaining in his lap in the meditation posture, indicating the moment he called the earth goddess Prithvi to witness his triumph over the demon Mara and his subsequent right to enlightenment, Maravijava.
While the undulation of the robe and the fall of the cloth in ridges over the legs maintains the early Ming style, the floral decoration of the borders is a later innovation of the fifteenth century. Compare the floral motif on the robe edges of the standing gilt-bronze figure of Amitabha in the British Museum, dated 3rd year of Chenghua, 1467, illustrated in Wladmimir Zwalf, ed., Buddhism: Art and Faith, London, 1985, cat. no. 302. Compare also the fall of the cloth from Amitabhaâs proper left shoulder ending in a single horizontal ridge at the crook of the elbow, evolved from the tripartite fold typical of earlier periods, seen on the Yongle (1403-1424) gilt bronze Buddha in the British Museum, ibid., cat. 305.

description_block:
The imposing Sino-Tibetan sculpting style of the present figure, its Nepalese-inspired cold-gilding and three inscriptions to its pedestal identify it as a rare imperial portrayal of the deity Vishnu, commissioned by the Qianlong Emperor (r. 1736-1795) for inclusion in one of his personal Buddhist halls. 
A devout Buddhist and follower of Tibetan Lamaist teachings, the Qianlong Emperor commissioned the production of a vast pantheon of Buddhist deities in parcel-gilt bronze, to be enshrined in eight Buddhist halls within his imperial palaces: four in the Forbidden City including the Baoxianglou and Fanhualou; three in the mountain resort of Chengde and one, the Fanxianglou, in the imperial Summer Palace. Each of these halls was divided into six sections, representing six subdivisions in Tibetan Buddhist practice: Prajnaparamita (Supreme wisdom); Supreme Yang tantra; Supreme Yin tantra; Yoga tantra, Charya Yoga, and Kriya Yoga; see Patricia Ann Berger, Empire of Emptiness: Buddhist Art and Political Authority in Qing China, Honolulu, 2003, p. 107.
The inscription on the front of the present pedestal Bianrutian ('The All-Pervading One') identifies the figure as Vishnu, while the aphorism on the rear, Dexing gen ben, associates the figure with the Charya Tantra, represented in the fifth chamber of the Buddhist halls.
Constructed on the orders of the Qianlong Emperor in 1772, the Fanhualou (âSanctuary of Buddhist Essenceâ) is the only surviving hall from this mammoth project to survive with most of its collection of images retained. The present copperplate engraving is one of a series of twelve known as The Pacification of Taiwan and depicts the Qing armyâs assault on Lin Shuangwenâs forces at Xiaobantian Mountain. The designs for the complete series were prepared by the Qing court painters Yang Dazhang, Jia Quan, Xie Sui, Zhuang Yude, Li Ming and Yao Wenhan, among others, and engraved and printed by the imperial workshops between the fifty-third and fifty-fifth years of the Qianlong reign (1788â1790). Originally bound as an album in a fitted case, the complete series comprised twelve plates. It was commissioned to commemorate the suppression of the Lin Shuangwen Rebellion in Taiwan between 1787 and 1788, depicting the principal battles of the campaign, the victorious armyâs return across the sea, and the imperial banquet given by the Qianlong Emperor in honour of Fukangâan, Hailancha and other meritorious officers. Each engraving is surmounted by an imperial poem composed by the Qianlong Emperor.
In the early 1760s, the Qianlong Emperor commissioned the Italian Jesuit Giuseppe Castiglione (1688â1766) and three other missionaries at court to prepare the designs for the first series of prints commemorating his military victories. Once completed, the drawings were sent to France to be engraved on copperplates, and the resulting prints were shipped back to Beijing between 1772 and 1775. The Qianlong Emperor was so pleased with the series that he subsequently commissioned similar commemorative prints following later military campaigns.
By the time of the Taiwan campaign, all four Jesuit painters involved in the first series had died, and the preparation of the designs was therefore entrusted to Chinese court painters. Yang Dazhang, Jia Quan, Xie Sui, Zhuang Yude, Li Ming and Yao Wenhan based their compositions on military reports submitted by Fukangâan. The designs were subsequently engraved and printed in the workshops of the Imperial Household Department between 1788 and 1790. Unlike the earlier Conquests of the Western Regions, which had been sent to France for production, the designs, copperplates and impressions of The Pacification of Taiwan were all produced within the imperial workshops, reflecting the technical accomplishments of Qing craftsmen following their adoption of European copperplate-printing techniques. A complete set is preserved in the Palace Museum, Beijing.
Two complete sets of The Pacification of Taiwan were sold in our Hong Kong rooms: the first, from the collection of Lord Elgin, British Plenipotentiary to China, on 27th April 2003, lot 35; and the second on 9th October 2007, lot 131. A complete set in the Ethnologisches Museum, Berlin, is illustrated in Herbert Butz, Bilder fÃ¼r die Halle des Purpurglanzes, Berlin, 2003, pl. 26, together with an engraved copperplate, pl. 27. Three further engravings from the series are preserved in the MusÃ©e Guimet, Paris, illustrated in MichÃ¨le Pirazzoli-tâSerstevens, Gravures des ConquÃªtes de lâEmpereur de Chine Kâien-long au MusÃ©e Guimet, Paris, 1969, pp. 44â46.

description_block:
The present copperplate engraving is one of a series of four known as The Pacification of the Zhongmiao. Entitled Suppressing the Zhong Miao Tribes and Raising the Siege of Nanlong, it depicts the Qing army relieving the siege of Nanlong. The designs for the complete series were prepared by the court painter Feng Ning and others, and engraved and printed by the imperial workshops in the third year of the Jiaqing reign (1798). Originally bound as an album in a fitted case, the series comprised four plates, each surmounted by an imperial poem composed by the Qianlong Emperor, then Emperor Emeritus. The remaining three engravings depict The Capture of the Rebel Stronghold at Dongsa Dangzhang, The Capture of the Rebel Stronghold at Balin in the Northern District, and The Final Suppression of the Remaining Zhong Miao Forces.
Following the suppression of the Miao uprisings in Hunan and Guizhou in 1794, smaller-scale disturbances continued to occur throughout the region. In 1797, an uprising led by Wang Nangxian and others broke out in Nanlong, Guizhou, present-day Anlong. The Jiaqing Emperor consequently ordered Lebao, Governor-General of Yunnan and Guizhou, to command the campaign. The present engraving depicts Lebaoâs advance on Nanlong and the raising of the siege. Drawing upon Lebaoâs military report, the Qianlong Emperor composed an imperial poem of thirty-six rhymes recounting the Qing armyâs capture of Guanling, the relief of Xincheng, the taking of the Kazi River pass, and its subsequent advance from Puping across the river towards Nanlong. The poem also records the hardships endured by the soldiers and inhabitants during the six-month siege, when provisions and firewood were nearly exhausted, and the subsequent renaming of Nanlong prefecture as Xingyi following its relief.
The Pacification of the Zhong Miao continued the tradition of imperial battle imagery established during the Qianlong reign. Unlike The Victories over the Dzungars and Muslims, whose designs were prepared by Jesuit artists and sent to France for engraving, the present series is more distinctly rooted in Chinese pictorial traditions. Densely layered mountains, forests and rocks frame settlements arranged along the contours of the landscape, while soldiers and military encampments are dispersed throughout the composition. Finely engraved lines evoke the texture strokes and tonal effects of Chinese painting and traditional woodblock printing. The series thus both perpetuates the Qing court tradition of commemorative military imagery and exemplifies the integration of Chinese painting and printmaking with European copperplate engraving.

description_block:
The present album records the mountains and waterways, walled cities, roads and administrative divisions of Sichuan, accompanied by explanatory texts. The designation zongyu tushuo indicates that the work was intended not merely to represent the provinceâs geography pictorially, but also to continue the gazetteer tradition in which maps and written descriptions complement one another.
Local government offices of the Qing dynasty attached considerable importance to the compilation and preservation of maps. Such works served to clarify the administrative relationships between prefectures, sub-prefectures and counties, while also providing information concerning postal routes, communications, strategically important terrain, frontier administration and military logistics. Unlike printed maps circulated through provincial gazetteers, manuscript maps produced by government offices were generally compiled for specific administrative purposes and in limited numbers. Executed in colour on silk and explicitly inscribed as having been established by the Sichuan Governor-Generalâs Office, the present album was evidently closely associated with the provincial administration rather than intended for general circulation.
The forty-first year of the Qianlong reign coincided with the conclusion of the Second Jinchuan Campaign. Beginning in 1771, the Qing court conducted a major military campaign in northwestern Sichuan, culminating in the pacification of the Greater and Lesser Jinchuan territories in 1776. These years of warfare heightened official interest in the provinceâs topography, transport routes and frontier administration. Produced in the same year, shortly after the conclusion of the campaign, the present album reflects the contemporary concern with the geographical understanding and governance of Sichuan. It therefore constitutes not only an important geographical document, but also a compelling testament to the Qing administrationâs efforts to comprehend and govern the province during the Qianlong period.
The geographical landscape is rendered according to traditional Chinese cartographic conventions, emphasising the relationships between mountain ranges, waterways, cities and routes rather than employing the fixed scale and geographical coordinates characteristic of Western cartography. Mountains are delineated using techniques derived from landscape painting, while rivers wind across the compositions and place names and related annotations are inscribed directly onto the maps. This combination of practical information and pictorial expression is a defining feature of official Chinese regional cartography during the Qing dynasty.
Precisely dated and bearing a clear reference to the institution responsible for its production, this album preserves an official Qing understanding of Sichuanâs geographical landscape while illustrating the administrative, military and artistic functions of regional cartography in eighteenth-century China.

description_block:
Impressive in both scale and richly cast decoration, the present pair of vases exemplifies the grandeur of bronze vessels produced for the imperial court during the Qianlong reign. Their imposing form draws upon the ancient ritual bronze hu, the pear-shaped bodies densely cast in relief with powerful five-clawed dragons writhing amongst scrolling clouds and the necks flanked by dragon-form handles suspending loose rings. This combination of an archaistic form with the dynamic imagery of Qing imperial art reflects the Qianlong court's enduring fascination with antiquity and its creative reinterpretation. 
Vases of this monumental type would have formed part of five-piece altar garnitures, generally comprising a censer, a pair of candlesticks and a pair of vases, commissioned for ritual use in temples associated with the imperial court and often presented as tribute to the emperor. Their considerable scale and weight, together with the densely cast decoration, would have lent such ensembles an imposing presence during ceremonial observances. See a closely related five-piece Qianlong-marked bronze altar garniture, comprising two vases of this type, a censer and two candlesticks, sold in our Hong Kong rooms, 11th April 2008, lot 2826. The use of similarly monumental bronze garnitures within the Forbidden City is further documented by an undecorated set preserved in the Xianruo Temple, in the garden of Cining Gong (Palace of Compassion and Tranquillity), where the empress and imperial consorts conducted Buddhist ceremonies, illustrated in Qingdai gongting shenghuo, Hong Kong, 1985, pl. 467. 
Several closely related Qianlong-marked bronze vases are known. Compare an example from the F. Gordon Morrill Collection, sold at Christieâs Hong Kong, 28th November 2012, lot 2254; two further examples sold in these rooms, 9th November 2016, lot 142, and 8th November 2017, lot 46; a smaller example, lacking one handle, sold in the same rooms, 11th May 2011, lot 254; and a larger pair sold at Christieâs London, 15th May 2012, lot 188. Compare also a pair of monumental vases of related form from the Alfred Morrison Collection, cast with phoenixes in place of dragons, possibly suggesting that they were commissioned as tribute to the Qianlong Emperor's mother, sold at Christieâs London, 9th November 2004, lot 17. For another variation on monumental imperial bronze altar vases, see a pair of square-section vessels cast with dragons and phoenixes and made for one of the buildings of the Yuanming Yuan (Imperial Summer Palace), sold in our Hong Kong rooms, 29th/30th April 1997, lot 730, 10th April 2006, lot 1537, and again 9th October 2007, lot 1322.

Letter:To Chairman Mao,
It has been a long time since I last wrote to enquire after you.
I trust that you are in excellent health. I have recently heard that you have personally embraced frugality, reducing your food consumption and thereby setting an example for the whole nation. Though one who has fought through countless hardships, you remain steadfast in the principle of placing concern before enjoyment. Only a great leader could act in this way. Our government already possesses the characteristics of what Marx called a âcheap government.â Now, with economy practised ever more rigorously and frugality carried still further, the Chinese people are immeasurably fortunate.
Yet even the greatest virtue may have minor blemishes; amid such exemplary integrity, there may still be unworthy individuals who seek personal gain through corruption.
I have inspected the premises of the Hall of Literature and History at Jingxinzhai. The property itself is not in particularly poor condition, yet its management expenses are reportedly reckoned in the tens of millions. I do not know whether this is accurate. Many members of the Hall are now discussing the matter and suspect that the figures are fictitious. If they are indeed false, this would inevitably tarnish the governmentâs admirable administration.
The third kitchen of the Institute of Political Studies at the Peopleâs Revolutionary University has also been poorly managed. Before May of this year, neither the flour sacks nor the interest accrued on surplus funds was entered in the accounts; these were recorded as income only after the students made inquiries. Everyday vegetables are charged at market prices rather than wholesale prices, and the cadres responsible may not have been entirely truthful or scrupulous in their handling of the matter. Many students harbour doubts but dare not speak. This, too, runs contrary to the governmentâs benevolent intention of providing favourable treatment to its students.
The present session is now drawing to a close. I hope that improvements will be made when the fourth session is convened. There are also shortcomings in other respects, particularly in the course of study, which cannot be explained in just a few words.
I have recently suffered from haemorrhoids, which persisted for more than ten days, but I nevertheless managed to complete my ideological self-assessment. As for Yu Yiâs studies, thanks to your approval, arrangements have now been made with the Institute of Political Studies, and Brother Yu has been informed. I mention this for your information.
Sincerely,

Crisply moulded with two vibrant blooms surrounded by a tangled profusion of overlapping leaves, the present dish represents one of the finest examples of moulded designwork from the zenith of production at Ding kilns of Hebei. Feather-light in the hand yet imposing in its elegance, the dish bears all of the features of the finest Ding wears, from its unctuous ivory-white glaze to the fineness of the clay body beneath.
The present dish is particularly remarkable in its barbed rim design, which lends the piece a grandeur not dissimilar to later imperial porcelain designs of the Early Ming dynasty. Surviving examples of this form are exceedingly rare. Compare a larger dish of barbed rim and moulded bird design in the Museum of Oriental Ceramics, Osaka, in Chugoku no toji [Chinese ceramics], vol. 5: Hakuji [White ware], Tokyo, 1998, pl. 55; and another dish of more comparable size and rock and flower design, sold at Christie's New York, 5th June 1986, lot 189 and again in our New York rooms, 15th September 2015, lot 34. 
A related group of small dishes of fluted âchrysanthemumâ rims, lacking some of the finesse of the present barbed form, include a dish of related floral design excavated from a Ding kiln site in Xiheliu, Quyang county, in Ding ci yishu [The art of Ding porcelain], Shijiazhuang, 2002, pl. 150; one of crane design also from the same site, pl. 194; and a third of sleeping deer design in the National Palace Museum, Taipei, pl. 196.
The present floral design is also rare and possibly represents an earlier prototype of a later three-peony design termed Ti 56 by Jan Wirgin; see Sung Ceramic Designs, Stockholm, 1970, p. 157 and pl. 100a for an example in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford. Compare also a sherd of very similar moulded floral style uncovered from Quyang in Selection of Ding Ware. The Palace Museum's Collection and Archaeological Excavation, Beijing, 2012, pl. 117.

description_block:
Paper-thin, wrinkled from years of treasured ownership and folded like book pages, gold leaves like the present, hammered from high-purity gold, served as currency in the Song dynasty during periods of cash shortage. Full leaves like the present served as a medium for large-scale trade and could be cut into smaller pieces as needed.
During the Southern Song dynasty, one tael of gold (roughly 40 grams) was worth 24,000 copper cashâ equivalent to a magistrate's monthly salary (roughly 40,000 yuan today). A single gold leaf could purchase 200 bolts of silk at the Port of Quanzhou or be exchanged for enough copper cash to hire 50 laborers for a month. Additionally, gold leaves were widely used by the public to pay in-kind taxes to the government.
The present leaf features four corner stamps reading Guanxiang Qianjie ('Front Street of Guanxiang'), one of the major gold-and-silversmith hubs in Southern Song Hangzhou, alongside Qinghefang Xi and Tianshuiqiao Dong. The central stamp, Xu Erlang Pu, identifies the specific workshop that crafted it.
Requiring smiths to stamp their trade names was effectively a government quality-assurance scheme: if a leaf was later found to be impure during circulation, the authorities could hold the workshop liable. An identical gold leaf, matching both inscription and shape, is preserved in the collection of the Hangzhou Museum, Hangzhou.

description_block:
This elegant marriage bowl exemplifies the refined craftsmanship and auspicious symbolism characteristic of jade carving during the Qianlong period. Skilfully carved from even-toned white jade, it is richly adorned with symbols of marital happiness and harmony: the shuangxi ('double happiness') character, the endless knot symbolizing binding and continuity, the musical stone qing, associated with celebration, and bat-form handles emblematic of good fortune. Adorned with such auspicious imagery, marriage bowls were popular wedding gifts among the scholarly elite and the imperial household. The deeply carved and pierced decoration, enhanced by the freely moving rings suspended from the handles, further demonstrates the technical virtuosity of Qing jade carvers.
Compare a similar white jade marriage bowl from the Alan and Simone Hartman Collection, illustrated in Robert Kleiner, Chinese Jades from the Collection of Alan and Simone Hartman, Hong Kong, 1996, pl. 67, and sold at Christieâs Hong Kong, 27th November 2007, lot 1539; a pale celadon jade example from the collection of Colonel Tom Hall (1928â2022), sold in our Paris rooms, 15th June 2023, lot 13; and another carved in white and russet jade from the collection of Sir John Woolf, illustrated in The Woolf Collection of Chinese Jade, London, 2013, pl. 63. Compare also a related example, smaller in size and carved with a shou character in place of the shuangxi character, in the Tianjin Museum, illustrated in Tianjin Bowuguan cang yu / Jade Wares Collected by Tianjin Museum, Beijing, 2012, pl. 189.

description_block:
This magnificent vase forms part of a rare and important group of large rouleau vases, almost twice as large as standard, produced towards the end of the Kangxi reign. Known for the particularly fine quality of their brushwork, the brilliance of their enamels and their bold and considered figural compositions, these vases appear to be the largest forms produced during the Kangxi period in the famille verte pallette and represent among the finest examples of the palette's use.
Surviving vases of this size are exceedingly rare. Compare five examples depicting dragon-boat scenes: one in R. L. Hobson, The Leonard Gow Collection of Chinese Porcelain, London, 1931, pl. XXV, cat. no. 126; the second sold in our New York rooms, 3rd June 1976, lot 478; the third sold in these rooms, 16th December 1990, lot 391; and two from the Altman Collection at the Metropolitan Museum of Art (14.40.83 and 85). Two further examples of this size from the Jie Rui Tang Collection are illustrated in Jeffrey Stamen and Cynthia Bolk, A Culture Revealed, Bruges, 2017, pls 1 and 60, the former most recently sold at Zhongxuan Shanghai, 26th April 2026, lot 637; and its pair, from the Saint Louis Art Museum, sold at Christie's New York, 30th March 2005, lot 396. Another, depicting a scene from the Sanguo Yanyi (Romance of Three Kingdoms), was sold twice in these rooms, 27th February 1973, lot 80 and 7th November 2007, lot 329, and again at Christie's New York, 23rd September 2022, lot 928.
The present scene depicts a young man and woman submitting before a warrior, who appears to dance in front of his tent. While the identity of the present scene has yet to be identified within the literary canon, it is likely derived from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms. Compare a smaller rouleau vase apparently depicting a variation on the same scene sold twice in these rooms, 9th May 1972, lot 105; and again, 16th May 1995, lot 71; and a lobed baluster vase from the collection of the British Royal Family in John Ayers, Chinese and Japanese Works of Art in the Collection of Her Majesty the Queen, vol. The present vase represents an usual, and likely early, piece of Yongzheng period (1723-1735) imperial porcelain, featuring the painterly style and flamboyant shape more familiar in the Kangxi period (1662-1722) and earlier Transitional period.
The inscription on the present vase, attributes its production to the Sanwei (lit. 'Three Fears') Hall, a monicker for the Lu family who served as local officials for the Yongzheng court. Stationed in the Jiangning region (modern-day Nanjing, Anhui and Shanghai), the Sanwei were founded by Lu Wen who identified three virtues by which his family should live: 'fear the dignity of heaven, fear the anger of earth, and fear the truth of heart.'
Four-character reign marks like the present are rare. Compare a meiping of closely related Yongzheng four-character mark and of period preserved in the Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated in The Complete Collection of Treasures of the Palace Museum, Blue and White Porcelain with Underglazed Red (III), Hong Kong, 2000, pl. 74, of closely related painterly blue and white painting style depicting birds on a withered branch.

description_block:
Remarkable for its monumental scale and finely painted decoration, the present charger is an impressive example of Kangxi blue and white porcelain. Measuring approximately 60 cm in diameter, its expansive surface provides an unusually ambitious pictorial field for the depiction of the 'Four Concubines', here shown gathered around a table in an elegant interior opening onto a garden landscape. Painted in varying tones of cobalt blue, the carefully arranged composition and surrounding landscape create a harmonious sense of depth and balance. 
Depictions of elegant ladies in refined domestic settings, surrounded by objects associated with scholarly pursuits, were a favoured subject on Kangxi porcelain. Such imagery drew upon the cultivated world traditionally associated with the scholar, transposed here to the private realm of female gatherings. The four figures on the present charger have been identified as the 'Four Concubines', traditionally referring to Jiang Yuan, Jiandi, Changyi and Qingdu, the four consorts of the legendary Emperor Ku, whose story is recorded as early as the Yiwen Leiju, the imperial encyclopaedia compiled under Ouyang Xun (557-641) and completed in 624. Rarely, however, does the subject appear on porcelain of this exceptional scale. A similar charger of the same impressive size and composition was sold in these rooms, 12th July 2006, lot 81. For another Kangxi representation of the subject, see a blue and white jar depicting the 'Four Concubines and Sixteen Children', illustrated in Kangxi Porcelain Wares from the Shanghai Museum Collection, Hong Kong, 1998, cat. no. 54. 
The production of a charger of such exceptional dimensions demanded considerable technical mastery: the potter had to control the large body through firing without warping, while the painter was faced with the challenge of maintaining the scale and proportions of an elaborate figural composition across its broad surface. Compare another monumental blue and white charger, formerly in the Morpurgo Collection, of the same size and framed by a similar ruyi border, but depicting Emperor Xuanzong visiting the Moon Palace, sold in these rooms, 8th November 2018, lot 5, and again at China Guardian, Beijing, 27th September 2022, lot 2049. Despite their different narrative subjects, the close correspondence in scale, border design and treatment of the figures suggests that the two chargers belong to a closely related group of monumental Kangxi blue and white wares.

description_block:
The present dish possesses a number of highly peculiar features, that typify the experimental production of the so-called 'Transitional period' and the first decade or so of the Kangxi reign (1662-1722), particularly in its form and the vibrancy of its finely painted polychrome enamel design. Depicting a lady framed with draping curtains, sat by a table beside a vase of prunus blossoms, the present design is also attested in a palette of underglaze blue and copper red on a similarly unusual larger basin, dated by its reign mark in accordance with 1671/2. This basin, now preserved in the National Gallery of Victoria, Melbourne (accession no. 617-D4), was sold from the property of S. D. Winkworth in these rooms, 27th April 1938, lot 253 and is illustrated in Teresa Canepa and Katharine Butler, Leaping the Dragon Gate. The Sir Michael Butler Collection of Seventeenth-Century Chinese Porcelain, London, 2021, p. 418, fig. III.4.68, where the authors identify the design as a scene from the Xixiangji (Romance of the Western Chamber).
For another early Kangxi dish of the present squat form and heavy potting, compare a blue and white example in the Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated in Chen Runmin, ed., Qing Shunzhi Kangxi chao qinghua ci, Beijing, 2005, pl. 77, where the author describes the form as a Ming Wanli period innovation, perfected and refined in the Kangxi.

description_block:
Large porcelain incense burners like the present, inspired in form by archaic bronze ding tripods, were made in a range of colours as part of sumptuously decorated altar garnitures for the imperial palaces of Beijing and Chengde, alongside candlesticks, gu beaker vases and occasionally other Tibetan metalware-inspired forms. These garnitures appear to have been first formalised in the Qianlong period (1736-1795) but continued to be produced and refined in the ensuing reigns, particularly those of the Jiaqing (1796-1820) and Daoguang (1820-1850) Emperors.
Compare a closely related censer of Jiaqing mark and period with a lime-green ground in place of the present turquoise, sold as part of a complete five-piece garniture in our New York rooms, 16th March 2016, lot 308; a yellow-ground example sold individually in our Hong Kong rooms, 3rd October 2017, lot 3715; and another lime-green example sold at Christie's London, 8th November 2011, lot 412.

The square seal Xu Yunlin zhi stamped on to the back of the figure belongs to Xu Youyi (1887-1940), the principal follower, pupil and associate of the master Dehua potter Su Xuejin (1869-1919). As John Ayers explains (see Blanc de Chine. Divine Images in Porcelain, China Institute Gallery, New York, 2002, p. 121), the superb quality of Xu Youyi's work previously led scholars to assume a late eighteenth century date. His works characterised by elaborate details and a consistent milky-white glaze, Xu came from a family of wood carvers and clay sculptures and his pieces remain beloved today. description_block:
Of vibrant imperial design and magnificent size, the present dish is a fine and rare example of pieces marked for use in the Chuxiugong (Palace of Gathering Elegance). Located in the northwest of the Forbidden City, and originally constructed in the fifteenth century, the palace was a favourite of the Empress Dowager Cixi, who established it as her chief residence between 1856 and 1885.
Porcelains featuring the present toponymous Chuxiugong zhi mark appear to have been produced as imperial gifts rather than for daily use and may have been commissioned en masse by the Empress Dowager; see Chen Kelun, 'Huafan jinse yongqing Changchun. Cixi he tade yuyong ciqi [Flourishing blossoms and splendid colors. Cixi and her imperial porcelain]', Forbidden City, September 2019, p. 134. As Ronald W. Longsdorf notes ('The Tongzhi Imperial Wedding Porcelain', Orientations, October 1996, p. 70), Cixi is known to have renovated the Chuxiugong in 1884 on the occasion of her 50th birthday and adorned it with sumptous decorations and monumental wares often modeled after eighteenth century prototypes.
In this regard, the present charger is no exception. Featuring dragons in pursuit of flaming pearls in green enamel on an underglaze-blue ground, the design of the present charger faithfully reproduces a beloved Kangxi period (1662-1722) prototype and speaks to Cixi's dedication to imperial continuity. Compare a smaller 'dragon' dish of the present design of Kangxi mark and period in the Fondation Baur, Geneva, illustrated in John Ayers, The Baur Collection. Chinese Ceramics, vol. IV, Geneva, 1974, pl. A555; and another sold at Christie's Hong Kong, 1st June 2016, lot 3236.
Surviving examples of this magnificent design are rare and are attested in three size variations: those measuring 32 cm in diameter, including one from the Kwan Collection, included in the exhibition The Splendour of Qing Dynasty, Hong Kong Museum of Art, Hong Kong, 1992, cat. no. 143, and sold at Christie's Singapore, 30th March 1997, lot 345, and another sold in our New York rooms, 18th September 2024, lot 168; larger dishes exceeding 70 cm in diameter, including one in the Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated in Chen Kelun, op. cit., p. 134; and another from the Barbara Jean Levy Collection, sold in our New York rooms, 20th September 2023, lot 569; and those of the present size (48 cm), including one sold in our Hong Kong rooms, 31st October and 1st November 1974, lot 295; and another sold at Christie's Hong Kong, 29th April 1996, lot 782.

provenance: Acquired by the grandfather of the present owner in Britain in the late 1950s or early 1960s, by family understanding, and thence by descent.
